column1: # Jāmiʿ al-ʿUlūm wa-l-Ḥikam — Hadith 35: “Do not envy one another… be, servants of Allah, brothers”

column2: From Abū Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “Do not envy one another; do not inflate prices against one another; do not hate one another; do not turn your backs on one another; and do not undercut one another's sales. Be, servants of Allah, brothers. The Muslim is the brother of the Muslim:

he does not wrong him, nor forsake him, nor lie to him, nor look down on him. Taqwā is here” — and he pointed to his chest three times — “It is evil enough for a man to look down on his Muslim brother. All of the Muslim is inviolable to the Muslim: his blood, his wealth and his honour.” Muslim reported it.
Muslim recorded this hadith through the narration of Abū Saʿīd, the freed slave of ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿĀmir ibn Kurayz, from Abū Hurayrah.
This Abū Saʿīd's name is not known. More than one person narrated from him, and Ibn Ḥibbān mentioned him in his Thiqāt, while Ibn al-Madīnī said: He is unknown.

Sufyān al-Thawrī reported this hadith, saying in it: from Saʿīd ibn Yasār, from Abū Hurayrah. He erred in saying “Saʿīd ibn Yasār”; it is in fact Abū Saʿīd, the freed slave of Ibn Kurayz. So said Aḥmad, Yaḥyā and al-Dāraquṭnī. Part of it has also been narrated by another route.
Al-Tirmidhī recorded it through the narration of Abū Ṣāliḥ, from Abū Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “The Muslim is the brother of the Muslim:

he does not betray him, lie to him or forsake him. All of the Muslim is inviolable to the Muslim: his honour, his wealth and his blood. Taqwā is here. It is evil enough for a man to look down on his Muslim brother.”
Abū Dāwūd recorded it from his words, “All of the Muslim…”, to the end.

Al-Bukhārī and Muslim recorded in the two Ṣaḥīḥs, through the narration of al-Aʿraj, from Abū Hurayrah, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Do not envy one another, do not inflate prices against one another, do not hate one another, do not turn your backs on one another, and be, servants of Allah, brothers.”
They also recorded it by other routes from Abū Hurayrah.
Imam Aḥmad recorded, from the hadith of Wāthilah ibn al-Asqaʿ, that the Prophet ﷺ said:

“All of the Muslim is inviolable to the Muslim: his blood, his honour and his wealth. The Muslim is the brother of the Muslim: he does not wrong him or forsake him. Taqwā is here” — and he pointed with his hand to the heart — “and it is evil enough for a man to look down on his Muslim brother.”
Abū Dāwūd recorded only the last part of it.
In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar, the Prophet ﷺ said: “The Muslim is the brother of the Muslim: he does not wrong him or abandon him to harm.”

Imam Aḥmad recorded it, in this wording: “The Muslim is the brother of the Muslim: he does not wrong him, forsake him or look down on him; and it is evil enough for a man to look down on his Muslim brother.”
In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from Anas, the Prophet ﷺ said: “Do not hate one another, do not envy one another, do not turn your backs on one another, and be, servants of Allah, brothers.”
Its meaning is narrated from the hadith of Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq, both as marfūʿ (attributed to the Prophet ﷺ) and as mawqūf on him (his own words).

His words ﷺ, “Do not envy one another,” mean: let none of you envy another. Envy is ingrained in human nature: it is a person's dislike of anyone of his own kind surpassing him in any kind of excellence.

After this, people fall into several groups. Some strive to bring about the loss of the envied person's blessing by transgressing against him in word and deed. Of these, some strive to transfer it to themselves,
and some strive only to remove it from the envied person without transferring it to themselves; this is the worse and the more vile of the two. This is the blameworthy envy that has been forbidden.

It was the sin of Iblīs, when he envied Ādam (peace be upon him) on seeing that he had surpassed the angels: Allah had created him with His hand, made His angels prostrate to him, taught him the names of all things and settled him in His nearness.
He did not cease striving to have him expelled from Paradise until he was expelled from it. It is narrated from Ibn ʿUmar that Iblīs said to Nūḥ:

With two things I destroy the children of Ādam: envy — and by envy I was cursed and made an accursed devil — and greed — and the whole of Paradise was made lawful to Ādam, yet through greed I got what I wanted from him.
Ibn Abī al-Dunyā recorded it.
Allah has described the Jews as envious in several places in His Book, the Qurʾān, such as His words, Exalted is He:

“Many of the People of the Book wish they could turn you back into disbelievers after your faith, out of envy from within themselves, after the truth has become clear to them” [al-Baqarah 2:109]; and His words: “Or do they envy people for what Allah has given them of His bounty?” [al-Nisāʾ 4:54].
Imam Aḥmad and al-Tirmidhī recorded, from the hadith of al-Zubayr ibn al-ʿAwwām, from the Prophet ﷺ: “The disease of the nations before you has crept into you: envy and hatred.

Hatred is the shaver — the shaver of religion, not the shaver of hair. By Him in whose hand is Muḥammad's soul, you will not believe until you love one another. Shall I not tell you of something that, if you do it, you will love one another?
Spread the greeting of peace among you.”
Abū Dāwūd recorded, from the hadith of Abū Hurayrah, that the Prophet ﷺ said:
“Beware of envy, for envy devours good deeds as fire devours firewood” — or he said: “grass.”

Al-Ḥākim and others recorded, from the hadith of Abū Hurayrah, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “The disease of the nations will strike my nation.” They said: Prophet of Allah, what is the disease of the nations?
He said: “Insolence, arrogance, vying for more, competing for this world, hating one another and envying one another, until there is transgression and then killing.”
Another group of people, when they envy someone, do not act on their envy and do not transgress against the envied person in word or deed.
It is narrated from al-Ḥasan that one does not sin by that, and this has been narrated as marfūʿ by weak routes. This is of two kinds.
The first is that he is unable to remove the envy from himself; he is overcome by it, and so does not sin by it.

The second is one who deliberately entertains it, turning it over again and again within himself and taking comfort in wishing that his brother's blessing would cease. This resembles a firm resolve to commit a sin,

and scholars differ over whether one is punished for that; it may be discussed elsewhere, if Allah the Exalted wills. But such a person is unlikely to keep from transgressing against the one he envies, if only in words, and so he sins by that.

Another group, when they envy, do not wish the envied person's blessing to cease, but strive to acquire excellences like his and wish to be like him. If the excellences are worldly, there is no good in that,

as those who desired the life of this world said: “If only we had the like of what Qārūn has been given” [al-Qaṣaṣ 28:79]. If they are religious excellences, it is good; the Prophet ﷺ himself wished for martyrdom in the path of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.
In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, he ﷺ said: “There is no envy except in two cases:

a man to whom Allah has given wealth, and he spends it through the hours of the night and the day; and a man to whom Allah has given the Qurʾān, and he stands in prayer with it through the hours of the night and the day.” This is wholesome emulation (ghibṭah), and he called it envy figuratively.
Another group, when they find envy in themselves, strive to remove it and to do good to the one they envy, by showing him kindness, praying for him

and spreading word of his merits, and by ridding themselves of the envy they find towards him, until they replace it with the wish that their Muslim brother be better and more excellent than they are.

This is among the highest degrees of faith, and the one who has it is the believer complete in faith, who loves for his brother what he loves for himself. We have already discussed this in explaining the hadith, “None of you believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself.”
His words ﷺ, “do not inflate prices against one another”: many scholars explained this as najsh in sales, which is when someone who does not want to buy an item bids up its price,
either to benefit the seller by raising its price for him, or to harm the buyer by making it dearer for him. In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from Ibn ʿUmar, the Prophet ﷺ forbade najsh.
Ibn Abī Awfā said: The one who practises najsh is a devourer of usury and a cheat. Al-Bukhārī mentioned it.
Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr said: They are agreed that whoever does it is disobeying Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, if he knows of the prohibition.

They differed over the sale itself. Some said it is invalid; this is a reported position of Aḥmad, chosen by a group of his followers. Others said: If the one bidding up is the seller, or someone the seller colluded with, the sale is invalid,
because the prohibition here relates to the contracting party himself; otherwise it is not invalid, because it relates to an outsider.
Likewise it is related that al-Shāfiʿī explained the sale's validity by the seller being someone other than the one bidding up.

Most jurists hold that the sale is valid in every case. This is the view of Abū Ḥanīfah, Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, and Aḥmad in one reported position — except that Mālik and Aḥmad gave the buyer the option of annulling if he did not know the circumstances

and was grossly overcharged beyond what is customary. Mālik and some of Aḥmad's followers set this at a third of the price. If the buyer then chooses to annul the sale, he may; and if he wants to keep it, the amount by which he was overcharged is deducted from the price. The scholars of our [Ḥanbalī] school have mentioned this.
The tanājush forbidden in this hadith may also be explained more broadly, for the root meaning of najsh in the language is stirring something up by scheming, trickery and deceit.

That is why the one who bids up prices in a sale is called a nājish, and in the language a hunter is also called a nājish, because he stirs up the game by trickery and deceit. On this view the meaning is: Do not deceive one another, and let none of you deal with another by scheming and trickery.

Scheming and deceit are aimed only at bringing harm to a Muslim, either directly, or by gaining some benefit for oneself that necessarily brings harm upon him. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has said: “But the evil plot encompasses none but its own people” [Fāṭir 35:43].
In the hadith of Ibn Masʿūd, from the Prophet ﷺ: “Whoever cheats us is not of us; scheming and deceit are in the Fire.”
We have already mentioned the marfūʿ hadith of Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq: “Accursed is whoever harms a Muslim or schemes against him.” Al-Tirmidhī recorded it.
On this reading, the forbidden tanājush includes every kind of dealing that involves cheating and the like, such as disguising and concealing defects, and adulterating good merchandise with bad,

and overcharging a trusting man who does not know how to bargain. In His Book, Allah the Exalted has described the disbelievers and the hypocrites as scheming against the prophets and their followers. And how excellent are the words of Abū al-ʿAtāhiyah:
There is no worldly good save with religion, / and religion is nothing but noble character.
Scheming and deceit belong in the Fire; / they are among the traits of the people of hypocrisy.
Scheming is permissible only against those whom it is permissible to harm, namely disbelievers at war, as the Prophet ﷺ said: “War is deception.”
His words ﷺ, “do not hate one another”: he forbade Muslims to hate one another for reasons other than Allah, out of personal whims. Allah has made the Muslims brothers, and brothers love one another

and do not hate one another. The Prophet ﷺ said: “By Him in whose hand is my soul, you will not enter Paradise until you believe, and you will not believe until you love one another. Shall I not direct you to something that, if you do it, you will love one another?
Spread the greeting of peace among you.” Muslim recorded it.
We have already mentioned hadiths forbidding hatred and envy of one another.
Allah has made unlawful for the believers whatever stirs up enmity and hatred between them, as He says:
“All that
Satan wants is to stir up enmity and hatred between you through wine and gambling, and to turn you away from the remembrance of Allah and from prayer. Will you not then desist?” [al-Māʾidah 5:91].

He has reminded His servants of His favour in bringing their hearts together, as the Exalted says: “And remember the favour of Allah upon you, when you were enemies and He brought your hearts together, so that by His favour you became brothers” [Āl ʿImrān 3:103];

and He says: “It is He who supported you with His help and with the believers, and brought their hearts together. Had you spent all that is on earth, you could not have brought their hearts together, but Allah brought them together” [al-Anfāl 8:62–63].

For this reason, going about spreading tales has been made unlawful, because it stirs up enmity and hatred; and lying has been allowed for the sake of setting things right between people. Allah has encouraged setting things right between them, as the Exalted says:

“There is no good in much of their private talk, except for one who enjoins charity, or what is right, or setting things right between people; and whoever does that seeking the good pleasure of Allah, We shall give him a great reward” [al-Nisāʾ 4:114];
and He says: “And if two parties of the believers fight, then make peace between them” [al-Ḥujurāt 49:9]; and He says: “So fear Allah and set right what is between you” [al-Anfāl 8:1].
Imam Aḥmad, Abū Dāwūd and al-Tirmidhī recorded, from the hadith of Abū al-Dardāʾ, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Shall I not tell you of what is higher in degree than prayer, fasting and charity?”
They said: Certainly, Messenger of Allah. He said: “Setting right relations between people;
for corrupted relations between people are the shaver.”
Imam Aḥmad and others recorded, from the hadith of Asmāʾ bint Yazīd, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Shall I not tell you who are the worst of you?”
They said: Certainly, Messenger of Allah. He said: “Those who go about spreading tales, who separate loved ones, and who seek to bring hardship on the innocent.”
As for hatred for the sake of Allah, it is one of the firmest handholds of faith and is not included in the prohibition. If some evil appears to a man from his brother, and he hates him for it,
while in reality the man is excused, the one who hated him is rewarded, even though his brother is excused. As ʿUmar said: We used to know you while the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was among us,

while revelation was coming down and Allah was informing us of your news. But the Messenger of Allah ﷺ has been taken away and revelation has ceased, so we know you only by what we learn of you by experience.

Whoever of you shows us good, we think well of him and love him for it; and whoever of you shows us evil, we think ill of him and hate him for it. Your secrets are between you and your Lord, the Mighty and Majestic.

Al-Rabīʿ ibn Khuthaym said: If you saw a man showing good and concealing evil and loved him for it, Allah would reward you for loving good; and if you saw a man showing evil and concealing good and hated him for it, Allah would reward you for hating evil.

When people's disagreements over questions of religion grew many and their divisions multiplied, their hatred and cursing of one another multiplied because of it. Each of them makes out that he hates for the sake of Allah. He may in reality be excused, and he may not be excused,

but be following his own desire and falling short in investigating what he hates others for. Much hatred of this kind arises only from disagreement with someone followed whom one thinks says nothing but the truth — and that belief is certainly mistaken;

or, if what is meant is that he says nothing but the truth in the particular matter in which he was disagreed with, that belief may be mistaken or correct. What drives one's partisanship may be mere desire, or familiarity, or habit, and all of this undermines the claim that this hatred is for Allah.

The believer must therefore give himself sincere counsel and be as cautious as possible in this; and where something is unclear, he should keep out of it, for fear of falling into the unlawful hatred that has been forbidden.

There is a subtle matter here to which one should be alert. Many imams of the religion may hold a weaker view while exercising ijtihād in it, rewarded for their ijtihād and absolved of their error; yet the one who champions that view of theirs does not stand at the same rank,
because he may champion it only because the one he follows held it, so that had another of the imams of the religion held it, he would not have accepted it or championed it,
nor befriended those who agreed with it or treated as enemies those who disagreed. Yet he thinks that he is championing the truth just as the one he follows was; and that is not so.

The one he follows intended only to champion the truth, even if he erred in his ijtihād. This follower's championing of what he thinks is the truth, however, is mixed with the desire that the one he follows be exalted and his word prevail,

and that he not be charged with error. This is a hidden taint that undermines the intention of championing the truth. Understand this, for it is a great insight; and Allah guides whom He wills to a straight path.

His words, “do not turn your backs on one another”: Abū ʿUbayd said: Tadābur is breaking off relations and shunning, taken from a man turning his back (dubur) on his companion and averting his face from him; it is cutting each other off.

Muslim recorded, from the hadith of Anas, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Do not envy one another, do not hate one another, do not cut one another off, and be, servants of Allah, brothers, as Allah has commanded you.”
He also recorded something with its meaning from the hadith of Abū Hurayrah, from the Prophet ﷺ.

In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from Abū Ayyūb, the Prophet ﷺ said: “It is not lawful for a Muslim to shun his brother for more than three nights, the two of them meeting and each turning away from the other; the better of them is the one who greets first.”
Abū Dāwūd recorded, from the hadith of Abū Khirāsh al-Sulamī, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Whoever shuns his brother for a year, it is like shedding his blood.”

All this concerns breaking off relations over worldly matters. When it is for the sake of religion, it may go beyond three days; Imam Aḥmad stated this explicitly, citing the story of the three who stayed behind, whom the Prophet ﷺ ordered to be shunned when he feared hypocrisy from them.

He also permitted shunning people of grave innovations and those who call to heresies. Al-Khaṭṭābī mentioned that a father's shunning of his child, a husband's of his wife, and the like, as discipline, may go beyond three days,
because the Prophet ﷺ kept away from his wives for a month.
They differed over whether shunning is ended by the greeting of peace.

One group said that it is ended by it. This is narrated from al-Ḥasan, and from Mālik in the narration of Ibn Wahb, and a group of the scholars of our school held it. Abū Dāwūd recorded, from the hadith of Abū Hurayrah, that the Prophet ﷺ said:

“It is not lawful for a believer to shun a believer for more than three days. If three have passed, let him meet him and greet him. If he returns his greeting, they share in the reward; if he does not return it, he bears the sin, and the one who greeted is released from the shunning.”

But this concerns the case where the other refuses to return the greeting. Where he returns it, if there was affection between them before the shunning and they have not gone back to it, the matter is open to question.
Aḥmad was asked, in the narration of al-Athram, whether the greeting ends shunning,

and said: He may greet him and still have turned away from him. Then he said: The Prophet ﷺ says, “They meet, and this one turns away and that one turns away”; that is, when he had been in the habit of talking with him or shaking his hand.
Likewise it is narrated from Mālik that shunning is not ended without a return to affection.

Some distinguished between relatives and non-relatives, saying that between non-relatives shunning ends with the mere greeting, unlike between relatives; he said this only because maintaining ties of kinship is obligatory.
His words ﷺ, “and do not undercut one another's sales”: the prohibition of this is reported many times. In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from Abū Hurayrah,
the Prophet ﷺ said: “A man is not to sell over his brother's sale, nor propose marriage over his brother's proposal.”
In a narration of Muslim's: “A Muslim is not to bargain over a Muslim's bargaining, nor propose over his proposal.”

They recorded it from the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “A man is not to sell over his brother's sale, nor propose over his brother's proposal, unless he gives him leave.” The wording is Muslim's.

Muslim recorded, from the hadith of ʿUqbah ibn ʿĀmir, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “The believer is the brother of the believer, so it is not lawful for a believer to buy over his brother's sale, nor to propose over his brother's proposal, until he gives it up.”
This shows that it is a right that a Muslim has over a Muslim, in which a disbeliever is not his equal; a Muslim may buy over a disbeliever's sale and propose over his proposal.

This is the view of al-Awzāʿī and Aḥmad, just as in Aḥmad's view a disbeliever has no right of pre-emption against a Muslim. Many jurists held that the prohibition applies generally, to Muslim and disbeliever alike.

They differed over whether the prohibition expresses unlawfulness or dislike. Some of the scholars of our school said that it expresses dislike rather than unlawfulness; the correct view, held by the great majority of scholars, is that it expresses unlawfulness.
They differed over whether a sale over one's brother's sale, or a marriage over his proposal, is valid.

Abū Ḥanīfah, al-Shāfiʿī and most of the scholars of our school said that it is valid. Mālik said of marriage: If he has not consummated it, they are separated; if he has consummated it, they are not separated.
Abū Bakr, of our school, said of both sale and marriage that they are void in every case, and related this from Aḥmad.
Selling over one's brother's sale means that the brother has sold someone something, and he then offers the buyer his own goods so that he buys them and cancels the first sale.
Does this apply only when the offer is made during the option period, when the buyer is able to cancel, or does it apply generally, both during the option period and after it?

Scholars disagree on this. Imam Aḥmad related the disagreement in the narration of Ḥarb and inclined to the view that it applies in both cases; this is the view of a group of the scholars of our school.
Some restricted it to the option period; this is the apparent sense of Aḥmad's words in the narration of Ibn Mushaysh, and the explicit position of al-Shāfiʿī. The first view is the sounder,
because even if the buyer cannot cancel on his own after the option period has ended, once he wants to return the first goods to their seller,
he will contrive to return them by various means that harm the seller, if only by pressing him with requests; and whatever leads to harm to a Muslim is unlawful. And Allah knows best.

His words ﷺ, “and be, servants of Allah, brothers”: the Prophet ﷺ mentioned this as a kind of reason for what preceded. It indicates that if they give up envying one another, inflating prices against one another, hating one another, turning their backs on one another and undercutting one another's sales, they will be brothers.

It also contains a command to acquire whatever makes Muslims brothers in every respect. This includes fulfilling the rights a Muslim has over a Muslim: returning his greeting, invoking mercy on him when he sneezes, visiting him when he is ill, following his funeral, accepting his invitation, greeting him first when meeting him, and wishing him well in his absence.
In al-Tirmidhī, from Abū Hurayrah, the Prophet ﷺ said: “Give one another gifts, for a gift removes rancour from the breast.”
Others recorded it, in this wording: “Give one another gifts, and you will love one another.”
In the Musnad of al-Bazzār, from Anas, the Prophet ﷺ said: “Give one another gifts, for a gift draws out ill will.”
It is narrated from ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, who traced the hadith back to the Prophet ﷺ: “Shake hands with one another, for it removes enmity; and give one another gifts.”
Al-Ḥasan said: Shaking hands increases affection.

Mujāhid said: It has reached me that when two who love each other meet, and one smiles at the other and they shake hands, their sins fall away as leaves fall from a tree. It was said to him: This is an easy deed.

He said: You call it easy, when Allah says: “Had you spent all that is on earth, you could not have brought their hearts together, but Allah brought them together; indeed He is Mighty, Wise” [al-Anfāl 8:63].
His words ﷺ: “The Muslim is the brother of the Muslim: he does not wrong him, nor forsake him, nor lie to him, nor look down on him.”

This is taken from His words, Mighty and Majestic is He: “The believers are but brothers, so set things right between your two brothers” [al-Ḥujurāt 49:10]. Since the believers are brothers, they have been commanded to do among themselves whatever brings hearts together and unites them, and forbidden whatever makes hearts recoil from one another and fall apart; and this is part of that.

Moreover, it is a brother's way to bring benefit to his brother and keep harm away from him, and among the greatest harms that must be kept from a Muslim brother is wrongdoing. This is not restricted to the Muslim;

it is unlawful towards everyone. Wrongdoing was discussed at length in connection with the ḥadīth qudsī of Abū Dharr: “O My servants, I have made wrongdoing unlawful for Myself and have made it unlawful among you, so do not wrong one another.”

Part of this is a Muslim's forsaking his brother, for the believer is commanded to help his brother, as he ﷺ said: “Help your brother, whether he is a wrongdoer or wronged.” A man said: Messenger of Allah, I help him when he is wronged, but how do I help him when he is a wrongdoer?
He said: “You prevent him from wrongdoing; that is your help to him.”
Al-Bukhārī recorded it with this meaning from the hadith of Anas, and Muslim recorded it with this meaning from the hadith of Jābir.
Abū Dāwūd recorded, from the hadith of Abū Ṭalḥah al-Anṣārī and Jābir ibn ʿAbdullāh, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “No Muslim forsakes a Muslim in a place where his sanctity is violated

and his honour impugned, but Allah will forsake him in a place where he would love His help; and no one helps a Muslim in a place where his honour is impugned and his sanctity violated, but Allah will help him in a place where he would love His help.”

Imam Aḥmad recorded, from the hadith of Abū Umāmah ibn Sahl, from his father, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Whoever sees a believer humiliated in his presence and does not help him, though he is able to, Allah will humiliate him before all creation on the Day of Resurrection.”

Al-Bazzār recorded, from the hadith of ʿImrān ibn Ḥuṣayn, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Whoever helps his brother in his absence, being able to help him, Allah will help him in this world and the Hereafter.”

Part of it too is a Muslim's lying to his brother: it is not lawful for him to tell him something and lie to him; he should tell him only the truth. In the Musnad of Imam Aḥmad, from al-Nawwās ibn Samʿān,
the Prophet ﷺ said: “It is a great betrayal that you tell your brother something in which he believes you while you are lying to him.”

Part of it too is a Muslim's looking down on his Muslim brother, which springs from arrogance, as the Prophet ﷺ said: “Arrogance is spurning the truth and looking down on people.” Muslim recorded it from the hadith of Ibn Masʿūd,

and Imam Aḥmad recorded it. In one of his narrations: “Arrogance is scorning the truth and despising people”; in another: “and belittling (ghamṣ) people”; and another adds: “so that he regards them as nothing.” Ghamṣ al-nās means disparaging and despising them.

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has said: “O you who believe, let not a people mock another people; perhaps they may be better than them; nor women mock other women; perhaps they may be better than them” [al-Ḥujurāt 49:11].

The arrogant man looks at himself with an eye that sees perfection, and at others with an eye that sees deficiency; so he looks down on them and despises them, and does not regard them as worthy of having their rights fulfilled by him, or of his accepting the truth from any of them when they bring it to him.

His words ﷺ, “Taqwā is here,” as he pointed to his chest three times, indicate that people's nobility in the sight of Allah lies in taqwā. Many a person whom people look down on for his weakness and his meagre share of this world

is greater in standing with Allah the Exalted than one who has standing in this world; for people differ only by taqwā, as Allah the Exalted says: “The noblest of you in the sight of Allah is the most God-fearing of you” [al-Ḥujurāt 49:13]. The Prophet ﷺ was asked: Who is the noblest of people?
He said: “The one among them who most fears Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.”
In another hadith: “Nobility is taqwā.” The root of taqwā is in the heart, as the Exalted says: “And whoever honours the rites of Allah — that is from the taqwā of the hearts” [al-Ḥajj 22:32].

This meaning was mentioned earlier, in discussing the ḥadīth qudsī of Abū Dharr, at his words: “If the first of you and the last of you, the humans among you and the jinn among you, were all as the most God-fearing heart of any one man among you, that would add nothing to My dominion.”
Since the root of taqwā is in the hearts, no one sees its reality except Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, as he ﷺ said: “Allah does not look at your forms and your wealth,
but He looks at your hearts and your deeds.” So many a person who has a fine form, or wealth, or rank, or leadership in this world may have a heart empty of taqwā,

while someone who has none of these may have a heart full of taqwā, and so be nobler in the sight of Allah the Exalted. Indeed, that is what happens more often, as in the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from Ḥārithah ibn Wahb,

from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: “Shall I not tell you of the people of Paradise? Every weak person regarded as weak, who, if he swore by Allah, Allah would fulfil his oath. Shall I not tell you of the people of the Fire? Every coarse, strutting, arrogant man.”

In the Musnad, from Anas, the Prophet ﷺ said: “As for the people of Paradise, they are every weak person regarded as weak, dishevelled, in two worn garments, who, if he swore by Allah, Allah would fulfil his oath;
and as for the people of the Fire, they are every haughty, strutting man who hoards and withholds, and has a retinue.”
In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from Abū Hurayrah, the Prophet ﷺ said: “Paradise and the Fire disputed. The Fire said: I have been favoured with the arrogant and the tyrants. Paradise said:

None enter me but the weak and the lowly among people. Allah said to Paradise: You are My mercy, through which I show mercy to whom I will of My servants; and He said to the Fire: You are My punishment, through which I punish whom I will of My servants.”

Imam Aḥmad recorded it from the hadith of Abū Saʿīd, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: “Paradise and the Fire boasted. The Fire said: My Lord, the tyrants, the arrogant, kings and nobles enter me. Paradise said: My Lord, the weak, the poor and the destitute enter me.” And he mentioned the rest of the hadith.
In Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, from Sahl ibn Saʿd, who said: A man passed by the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he said to a man sitting with him: “What do you think of this man?”

He said: He is one of the nobility; by Allah, this one deserves, if he proposes, to be married; if he intercedes, to have his intercession accepted; and if he speaks, to be listened to. The narrator said:
The Prophet ﷺ was silent. Then another man passed by, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to him: “What do you think of this one?”
He said: Messenger of Allah, this is one of the poor Muslims. This one deserves, if he proposes, not to be married; if he intercedes, not to have his intercession accepted;
and if he speaks, not to be listened to. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “This one is better than an earthful of the likes of that one.”

Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Quraẓī said of His words, Exalted is He: “When the Event befalls — there is no denying its befalling — lowering, raising” [al-Wāqiʿah 56:1–3]: It lowers men who were high in this world and raises men who were low in this world.

His words ﷺ, “It is evil enough for a man to look down on his Muslim brother,” mean that looking down on his Muslim brother is evil enough for him; for he looks down on his Muslim brother only out of arrogance towards him,
and arrogance is one of the gravest of evil traits. In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, the Prophet ﷺ said: “No one in whose heart is an atom's weight of arrogance will enter Paradise.”

It also has, from him, that he said: “Might is His lower garment and pride His cloak; whoever contends with Me over them, I will punish him.” Contending with Allah the Exalted over His attributes, which are not fitting for a created being, is evil enough.
In Ṣaḥīḥ Ibn Ḥibbān, from Faḍālah ibn ʿUbayd, the Prophet ﷺ said: “There are three about whom no question will be asked:

a man who contends with Allah over His lower garment, a man who contends with Allah over His cloak — for His cloak is pride and His lower garment is might — and a man in doubt about the command of Allah and despairing of the mercy of Allah.”
In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from Abū Hurayrah, the Prophet ﷺ said: “Whoever says, The people are ruined, is himself the most ruined of them.” Mālik said:

If he says it out of grief at what he sees in people — meaning in their religion — I see no harm in it; but if he says it out of self-admiration and contempt for people, that is the disliked thing that has been forbidden.
Abū Dāwūd mentioned this in his Sunan.

His words ﷺ, “All of the Muslim is inviolable to the Muslim: his blood, his wealth and his honour”: this is one of the things the Prophet ﷺ used to proclaim in his sermons at great gatherings. He proclaimed it in the Farewell Pilgrimage on the Day of Sacrifice,

on the Day of ʿArafah, and on the second of the Days of Tashrīq, saying: “Your blood, your wealth and your honour are inviolable to you, as inviolable as this day of yours, in this month of yours, in this land of yours.” In a narration of al-Bukhārī's and others: “and your skins.”
In one narration: He repeated it several times, then raised his head and said: “O Allah, have I conveyed it?
O Allah, have I conveyed it?”
In one narration: Then he said: “Let the one present among you convey it to the one absent.”
In a narration of al-Bukhārī's: “For Allah has made your blood, your wealth and your honour inviolable to you, except by their due right.”

In one narration: “Your blood, your wealth and your honour are inviolable to you, like this day and this land, until the Day of Resurrection — even a shove that a Muslim gives a Muslim, intending harm by it, is unlawful.”

In one narration he said: “The believer is inviolable to the believer, as inviolable as this day: his flesh is unlawful to him, to eat it by backbiting him in his absence; his honour is unlawful to him, to tear it; his face is unlawful to him, to slap it; his blood is unlawful to him, to shed it; and it is unlawful to him to give him a shove that distresses him.”
In the Sunan of Abū Dāwūd, from some of the Companions: they were travelling with the Prophet ﷺ, and one of them fell asleep.
Some of them went to a rope he had and took it, and he woke in fright. The Prophet ﷺ said: “It is not lawful for a Muslim to frighten a Muslim.”

Aḥmad, Abū Dāwūd and al-Tirmidhī recorded, from al-Sāʾib ibn Yazīd, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Let none of you take his brother's staff, whether in jest or in earnest; whoever takes his brother's staff, let him return it to him.”
Abū ʿUbayd said: He means that one takes something without intending to steal it, intending only to vex him; so he is jesting as far as theft goes, but in earnest in causing him harm and alarm.
In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from Ibn Masʿūd, the Prophet ﷺ said: “When you are three, two should not converse privately apart from the third, for that grieves him.” The wording is Muslim's.

Al-Ṭabarānī recorded, from the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Two should not converse privately apart from the third, for that hurts the believer, and Allah dislikes the hurting of the believer.”
Imam Aḥmad recorded, from the hadith of Thawbān, that the Prophet ﷺ said:

“Do not hurt the servants of Allah, do not reproach them, and do not seek out their faults; for whoever seeks out the faults of his Muslim brother, Allah will seek out his faults until He exposes him in his own house.”
In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from Abū Hurayrah: the Prophet ﷺ was asked about backbiting, and he said: “Your mentioning your brother with what he dislikes.” He said: What if what I say is in him?
He said: “If what you say is in him, you have backbitten him; and if what you say is not in him, you have slandered him.”

All these texts establish that it is not lawful to bring harm to a Muslim in any way, by word or deed, without right. Allah the Exalted has said: “And those who harm believing men and believing women for something they have not earned have borne the guilt of slander and manifest sin” [al-Aḥzāb 33:58].
Allah made the believers brothers only so that they would be compassionate and merciful to one another. In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from al-Nuʿmān ibn Bashīr, the Prophet ﷺ
said: “The likeness of the believers in their mutual love, mercy and compassion is that of the body: when one limb of it suffers, the rest of the body responds to it with fever and sleeplessness.”
In a narration of Muslim's: “The believers are like one man: if his head suffers, the rest of the body responds to it with fever and sleeplessness.”
Also in a narration of his:
“The Muslims are like one man: if his eye suffers, all of him suffers; and if his head suffers, all of him suffers.”
In both of them, from Abū Mūsā, the Prophet ﷺ said: “The believer to the believer is like a building, one part strengthening another.”

Abū Dāwūd recorded, from the hadith of Abū Hurayrah, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “The believer is the mirror of the believer. The believer is the brother of the believer: he protects him from loss and guards him from behind.”
Al-Tirmidhī recorded it, in this wording: “Each of you is his brother's mirror; if he sees something harmful on him, let him remove it from him.”
A man said to ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz: Treat the elderly among the Muslims as a father, the young as a son and those in between as a brother; then which of them would you want to treat badly?

Among the sayings of Yaḥyā ibn Muʿādh al-Rāzī: Let the believer's share from you be three things: if you do not benefit him, do not harm him; if you do not gladden him, do not grieve him; and if you do not praise him, do not disparage him.
